bib.title: Chapter 2: Multi-armed Bandits (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)

question: How should an agent balance exploration and exploitation when it learns from evaluative feedback in a single-state k-armed bandit?
hypothesis: Simple balancing methods (epsilon-greedy, optimistic initialisation, UCB, gradient bandit) work much better than always exploiting.
contributions: Defines the k-armed bandit, action values, greedy/exploring actions
Sample-average and incremental estimators, constant step size
epsilon-greedy, optimistic initial values, UCB1, gradient bandit (softmax preferences)
Contextual bandits as bridge to full RL

results.claim: Greedy method on the 10-armed testbed levels off at about 1 reward per step versus a best possible of about 1.54.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed: 2000 random k=10 bandits, q*(a)~N(0,1), rewards N(q*(a),1), 1000 steps per run, sample-average estimates with Q1=0 (Fig 2.2)
results.quote: It achieved a reward-per-step of only about 1, compared with the best possible of about 1.54 on this testbed.

results.claim: The best possible average reward on the testbed is about 1.54.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed: 2000 random k=10 bandits, q*(a)~N(0,1), rewards N(q*(a),1), 1000 steps per run, sample-average estimates with Q1=0
results.quote: compared with the best possible of about 1.54 on this testbed

results.claim: Greedy found the optimal action in only about one-third of tasks; in the other two-thirds it never returned to it after disappointing early samples.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed: 2000 random k=10 bandits, q*(a)~N(0,1), rewards N(q*(a),1), 1000 steps per run, sample-average estimates with Q1=0 (Fig 2.2 lower)
results.quote: the greedy method found the optimal action in only approximately one-third

results.claim: epsilon=0.1 never selected the optimal action more than 91% of the time.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed: 2000 random k=10 bandits, q*(a)~N(0,1), rewards N(q*(a),1), 1000 steps per run, sample-average estimates with Q1=0, epsilon=0.1 (Fig 2.2)
results.quote: but it never selected that action more than 91% of the time

results.claim: epsilon=0.01 improves more slowly than epsilon=0.1 but eventually performs better on both measures.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed: 2000 random k=10 bandits, q*(a)~N(0,1), rewards N(q*(a),1), 1000 steps per run, sample-average estimates with Q1=0, epsilon in {0, 0.01, 0.1}
results.quote: The " = 0.01 method improved more slowly, but eventually would perform better than the " = 0.1
results.note: Authors say 'would perform better'; the plotted 1000 steps do not show the crossover (stated, not measured).

results.claim: Optimistic greedy (Q1=+5, alpha=0.1) starts worse than realistic epsilon-greedy (Q1=0, epsilon=0.1) but ends better on the testbed.
results.quote: Initially, the optimistic method performs worse because it explores more, but eventually it performs better because its exploration decreases with time.

results.claim: UCB with c=2 beats epsilon-greedy epsilon=0.1 on the testbed except in the first k steps.
results.quote: UCB generally performs better than "-greedy action selection, except in the ﬁrst k steps

results.claim: Gradient bandit with a reward baseline is unaffected by shifting q*(a) to mean +4; without baseline performance is significantly degraded.
results.setup: 10-armed testbed variant, q*(a)~N(+4,1), alpha=0.1 and 0.4, with and without baseline (Fig 2.5)
results.quote: This shifting up of all the rewards has absolutely no e↵ect on the gradient bandit algorithm

results.claim: Parameter study: every algorithm has an inverted-U in its parameter and is fairly insensitive over about an order of magnitude; on this problem UCB seems best.
results.setup: Average reward over first 1000 steps on the 10-armed testbed; parameters varied by factors of two on a log scale, 1/128 to 4 (Fig 2.6)
results.quote: All of these algorithms are fairly insensitive, performing well over a range of parameter values varying by about an order of magnitude.
results.note: Fig 2.6 curve values are not printed in the text; read none.

results.claim: Gradient bandit updates equal gradient ascent on expected reward in expectation, so the algorithm is stochastic gradient ascent for any action-independent baseline.
results.quote: the expected update of the gradient bandit algorithm

results.claim: Exact Bayesian optimal exploration over a 1000-step horizon with two actions and two rewards has 2^2000 leaves in the tree.
Sample-average update has constant memory and computation: Q_{n+1} = Q_n + (1/n)[R_n - Q_n].
results.quote: which holds even for n = 1, obtaining Q2 = R1 for arbitrary Q1

results.claim: Constant step size alpha gives exponential recency-weighted average; convergence needs sum alpha_n = inf and sum alpha_n^2 < inf, which constant alpha fails.
results.quote: In fact, the weight decays exponentially according to the exponent

limits: Testbed is stationary, Gaussian, k=10; nonstationary experiments are left as exercises 2.5 and 2.11, not run.
Fig 2.6 values appear only as a plot; no table of numbers, no seeds, code or confidence intervals given.
Authors concede UCB is hard to extend to nonstationary problems and large state spaces with function approximation.
Authors concede the methods are far from a satisfactory solution to exploration/exploitation.
Optimistic initialisation is not suited to nonstationary problems; sample averages also treat the start of time specially.
practices: Use constant step size alpha for nonstationary problems (Sec 2.5).
Use incremental updates NewEstimate <- OldEstimate + StepSize[Target - OldEstimate] to keep constant memory (Sec 2.4).
Compare algorithms by a parameter study (average reward over 1000 steps vs parameter on log scale), not single settings (Sec 2.10).
Use a reward baseline in the gradient bandit; it lowers update variance without changing the expected update (Sec 2.8).
Optimistic initial values are a simple trick for stationary problems only (Sec 2.6).

Q_{n+1} = Q_n + (1/n)[R_n - Q_n];  NewEstimate <- OldEstimate + StepSize [Target - OldEstimate]
A simple bandit algorithm: Q(a)<-0, N(a)<-0; loop: A <- argmax_a Q(a) w.p. 1-eps (ties random), random action w.p. eps; R <- bandit(A); N(A)<-N(A)+1; Q(A)<-Q(A)+(1/N(A))[R-Q(A)]
